Our findings indicate that the transport physics of aligned polymers is governed by the topology of a single Q1D band within a simple band-filling framework and establish Hall measurements as a powerful tool for studying their charge transport physics.

title: Enterococcus faecalis biofilm rewires neutrophil metabolism to suppress antimicrobial activity
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Enterococcus faecalis
                    is an opportunistic pathogen that persists in biofilm-associated infections despite robust neutrophil recruitment. How
                    E. faecalis
                    evades neutrophils remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how
                    E. faecalis
                    biofilms alter effector functions in human neutrophils and a murine wound infection model. We found that
                    E. faecalis
                    biofilm suppresses neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, bacterial engulfment, and neutrophil-mediated control of biofilm growth. This suppression is partly driven by production of lactic acid through the lactate dehydrogenases (LDHs) of
                    E. faecalis
                    , which acidifies the extracellular environment, lowers neutrophil intracellular pH, and disrupts glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway. In a murine wound infection model, loss of LDH increased neutrophil recruitment and NETosis
                    .
                    We also found that high bacterial density, a defining feature of biofilms, suppresses NETosis through a lactic acid–independent mechanism. Collectively, these findings identify biofilm immune evasion strategies mediated by bacterial metabolism and the high-density structural organization of biofilm-associated bacteria.

title: Differential sex-dependent responses of circulating steroid hormones and cortical gene expression in a traumatic brain injury model
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Accumulating evidence supports sex differences in traumatic brain injury (TBI) outcomes. However, the underlying processes that lead to sex differences are not well understood. TBI results in the initiation of molecular and cellular responses that facilitate the progression of neurodegeneration. Little is known about how the circulating hormone profile is altered in response to TBI and whether sex differences in endocrine responses might shape secondary injury pathologies. Using intact male and female mice in a preclinical TBI model, we assessed changes in plasma hormone concentrations and cortical gene expression at 24 and 72 hours after TBI. We demonstrate that males and females exhibit sex-specific alterations in circulating levels of testosterone, androstenedione, estradiol, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) in response to TBI. We also identified sex differences in the expression of genes that are involved in immune responses and tissue remodeling after injury. Moreover, we report divergent circulating hormone and gene expression correlations between sexes.

title: Submesoscale feedback suppresses marine heatwaves
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are devastating extreme ocean temperature events whose frequency and severity have surged under global warming, threatening marine ecosystems and fisheries. Yet, the fundamental mechanisms that control their intensity and persistence remain incompletely understood. Here, using a submesoscale-permitting global model simulation validated by long-term observational and reanalysis data, this study reveals a previously overlooked submesoscale feedback that exerts a critical control on MHW severity. It is demonstrated that the submesoscale-induced vertical heat flux suppresses the intensity and persistence of atmosphere-driven MHWs in winter via a negative feedback mechanism. Enhanced air-sea net heat flux strengthens stratification and shoals the mixed layer, weakening submesoscale vertical heat transport by 19.4%, reducing MHW intensification by 18.1%, and accelerating decay by 21.7%. This missing regulatory mechanism indicates that models ignoring the submesoscale feedback likely overestimate MHW severity, with critical implications for future climate projections.

title: Observations show increased nitrate in coastal cloud droplet residuals from large-particle activation and N2O5 hydrolysis
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Clouds change the chemical composition of aerosols, yet observations characterizing these processes are quite limited. Ground-based in-cloud measurements in coastal Southern California show that the highest nitrate to sulfate ratio (2.5 ± 1.7) in droplet residuals is near cloud base where cloud liquid water content and droplet number concentration are below the observed 20th percentile. The number size distribution of nitrate-rich particles peaks at a larger diameter than sulfate-rich particles, supporting growth to droplets of nitrate-rich particles at lower supersaturations than for sulfate-rich particles. Nitrate mass concentrations are up to three times higher in-cloud compared to pre-cloud and correlated with statistically significant reductions in ozone concentrations, consistent with contributions from in-cloud nitrate formation by N
                    2
                    O
                    5
                    hydrolysis. This study provides quantitative relationships of cloud properties to nitrate production in droplet residuals and associated ozone reduction, illustrating the impacts of aqueous reactions in clouds.

title: All-soft organic electrochemical diodes based on asymmetric active layers for signal isolation in deformable electronics
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
All-soft electronics have emerged as a promising platform for deformable and human-centric systems, yet the development of mechanically compliant diodes remains a major challenge due to limitations in material compatibility, device architecture, and stable operation under deformation. Electrochemical approaches offer a viable route to address this challenge by enabling bulk, low-voltage charge modulation in soft materials without relying on rigid junction interfaces. Here, we report, to the best of our knowledge, the first all-soft organic electrochemical diode (OECD) based on an asymmetric active-layer geometry. The device incorporates a transfer-printed ultrathin ion-gel interface that preserves conformal coverage and the active electrochemical architecture under strain. The device achieves high rectification through polarity-dependent electrochemical potential redistribution, with a rectification ratio of up to 2.23 × 10
                    4
                    at ±1 V and stable operation under tensile strains of up to 30% and repeated mechanical deformation. This ion-gel-based architecture preserves the electrochemical asymmetry required for diode operation while maintaining structural integrity under strain. Beyond the individual device, the all-soft OECD enables deformable rectifiers and logic gates and functions as a key signal-isolation element that suppresses cross-talk in a deformable pressure-sensing array. These results establish an electrochemical diode platform that combines mechanical deformability, high rectification performance, and circuit-level compatibility, providing a pathway toward fully deformable and integrated human-centric electronic systems.

title: Physical confinement modulates the rate-limiting transition in the release of phosphate from actin filaments
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The nucleotide state and rates of transitions between states regulate the dynamics of ATPases. Slow inorganic phosphate (P
                    i
                    ) release following ATP hydrolysis is often rate limiting and associated with key conformational changes. Actin filaments offer a unique opportunity to understand the fundamentals of P
                    i
                    release because identical subunits at filament ends and the interior release P
                    i
                    at markedly different rates. The molecular origin of this difference is debated, so we used extensive all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize P
                    i
                    release from different subunits within an actin filament. The calculated dissociation rates of P
                    i
                    from ADP-Mg
                    2+
                    in the active site correlate with experimentally measured P
                    i
                    release rates and scale inversely with the numbers of water molecules in the cavity surrounding the γ-phosphate. Simulations show that egress of P
                    i
                    through the protein channels, including through the N111-R177 backdoor, is not rate limiting and that subunits at the filament ends use alternative egress pathways.

title: CREBBP loss drives immune evasion by epigenetically silencing STING and MHC-I in small cell lung cancer
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Most small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) exhibit low immunogenicity and intrinsic resistance to immunotherapy, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify
                    CREBBP
                    loss, a frequent genetic alteration in SCLC, as a key suppressor of tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses that drives an immune-cold tumor microenvironment in
                    Rb1/Trp53
                    -driven autochthonous mouse models. Consistently,
                    Crebbp
                    deletion promotes immune escape in syngeneic SCLC models. Mechanistically,
                    Crebbp
                    loss suppresses
                    Sting
                    and major histocompatibility complex class-I expression by reducing histone H3 acetylation. Notably, HDAC inhibition restores histone acetylation, reactivates these silenced genes, and induces tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses. Moreover, pharmacological HDAC inhibition synergizes with immune checkpoint blockade to suppress tumor growth in both
                    Crebbp
                    -mutant and
                    Crebbp
                    -wild-type SCLCs, with a more prominent effect in
                    Crebbp
                    -mutant tumors. Collectively, these findings establish
                    CREBBP
                    loss as a key mechanism of immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance in SCLC, highlighting HDAC inhibition as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

title: DMRT1 is required at two steps of ovarian differentiation in rabbits
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The transcription factor Doublesex and Mab-3 Related Transcription Factor 1 (DMRT1) is essential for testis differentiation and male fertility, but less is known about its potential involvement in ovarian differentiation. In mice,
                    Dmrt1
                    −/−
                    females are fertile, although they show a reduction of
                    Stra8
                    expression. Using our
                    DMRT1
                    mutant rabbit model, we analyzed ovarian differentiation when
                    DMRT1
                    expression is abolished. First, we observed that during early gonadal development,
                    DMRT1
                    −/−
                    gonads display a specific transcriptome different from control ovaries and control testes. Second, we assessed the infertility phenotype of mutant females. DMRT1 is highly expressed in germ cells until meiosis initiation, and its disruption leads to a down-regulation of key genes involved in the meiotic process. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing data highlighted that DMRT1 can bind these genes in the rabbit ovary. Our study using the rabbit model shows that in addition to its role in testicular differentiation, DMRT1 has two important functions in ovarian differentiation: an initial involvement in the differentiation of somatic cells and a pivotal role in the differentiation of germ cells. Our data suggested that DMRT1 could be considered in human health as a gene necessary for female fertility.

title: Validation of targets linked to weight gain in C57BL/6 mice and translational aspects in humans
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Obesity is linked to complex interactions between an organism’s genetic background and its environment. Mouse models have been invaluable research tools to study obesity, with C57BL/6N being widely studied, given its propensity for weight gain on a high-fat diet (HFD). Despite this, the genetic basis of its susceptibility is poorly understood. In a partner paper we have identified SNP variants in 11 genes causing susceptibility to, or protection against, HFD-induced obesity in male C57BL/6N mice explaining 87% of the individual variation in fat gain. Surprisingly, most of them were maximally expressed outside the brain. In this study, we further validate some of these targets. We demonstrate that tissue-specific inhibition of Nova1 and Mchr1 in muscle, Nr1i3 in liver, and Ahr in lung and liver led to resistance to HFD–induced obesity or glucose intolerance. Further RNAseq analysis revealed that mTOR, Acox1, IL-15, and eIF2a signals are positioned downstream of these genes, potentially mediating their effects on obesity susceptibility. Importantly, variants in eight of the genes identified here have been previously implicated in human obesity, suggesting that a deeper understanding of the genetic/environment interactions of model systems can inform this complex human disease. Our work confirms that body fat regulation is likely more complex than current models which focus on the brain–adipose axis suggest.

title: Translational control of microglial metabolism, inflammatory responses, and survival by the eIF4E-binding proteins
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes microglial neuroprotective functions by engaging multiple cell receptors. However, the relevant downstream effectors are not fully understood. mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) promotes mRNA translation by phosphorylating and inactivating eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 and 2 (4E-BP1/2), which are expressed in microglia. 4E-BP1 levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are elevated in AD and correlate with markers of microglial reactivity and disease progression. Using linear regression analysis, we found that elevated CSF 4E-BP1 levels strengthen the association between soluble TREM2 levels and neurodegeneration in amyloid-positive individuals. To investigate the underlying mechanism, we performed in vitro experiments demonstrating that amyloid-β inactivated 4E-BP1 in murine microglia. The mTOR-mediated inactivation is highly dependent on Spleen Tyrosine Kinase (SYK) signaling and repeated exposure to amyloid-β impaired this process, whereas prolonged exposure increased 4E-BP1 levels in microglia. Deletion of 4E-BP1/2 resulted in increased mitochondrial mass and oxidative phosphorylation, reduced pro-inflammatory signaling, and protected microglia from amyloid-induced apoptosis. Thus, impaired 4E-BP1 inactivation—due to reduced mTOR signaling or excess 4E-BP1—disrupts immune resolution, leading to metabolic exhaustion and microglial cell death. We identify the SYK–mTORC1–4E-BP1 signaling axis as a key regulator of microglial mitochondrial biogenesis and immune resolution in AD.

title: Linguistic intervention unlocks the economic gains of diversity
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Gains from trade generate prosperity, yet interpersonal exchange can falter along racial lines. We study incentivized experimental economies where participants must spontaneously initiate and sustain trading relationships with others whose race is visible. When the highest gains from trade require cross-race exchange, diverse economies underperform: welfare and specialization suffer as many retreat to autarky. This underperformance reflects not segregation into racial trading blocs, but a collapse in exchange. Opportunities for contact alone do not close the performance gap, which persists and even widens over time. To understand why, we turn to communication itself. Lower welfare is associated with less communication, fewer expressions of affiliation and achievement, and less explicit signaling of needs, deficits, and surpluses. We call this communicative misalignment: differences in shared-language use that raise search, bargaining, and coordination costs. A brief linguistic intervention equips participants with a communicative toolkit. It increases communication volume and the frequency of motivational and state-signaling language. Crucially, when gains depend on cross-race exchange, the intervention restores specialization and cross-race trade, closing the performance gap. Its effects are minimal when efficient trade need not cross race, indicating specificity rather than generic skill training. Language thus operates bidirectionally, both revealing the state of cooperation and causally shaping it. Although we examine racial boundaries, the mechanism may operate along other fault lines where interactional norms diverge, including hierarchy, geography, or culture. Language, a primary conduit of culture, can impede exchange when misaligned and facilitate it when aligned. This suggests a scalable micro-governance tool for reducing transaction costs.

title: Enhancing simulations of disordered protein ensembles with chemical shift restraints in coarse-grained models
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
With more than one third of the human proteome being structurally disordered, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are key contributors to complex cellular functions, despite their highly dynamic conformational ensembles remaining elusive to conventional techniques in structural biology. Coarse-grained (CG) simulation methods thus serve as a gold standard to refine IDP ensembles. These methods, when relying on elastic network models or rigid body to sample secondary structure, are however inherently limited in their capability to model and sample transient secondary structure at a residue-level resolution as informed by experimental data. This fundamental limitation persists despite experimental evidence suggesting that transient structural propensities are a fundamental hallmark of IDP function. Through an artificial neural network capable of predicting backbone chemical shifts from C
                    α
                    -only protein conformations, we present a generalized framework which does not rely on dihedral parameterization to equip one bead-per-aminoacid CG force fields with the ability to sample functional elements of secondary structure. When applied on a large set of IDPs in isolation or condensates, our approach correctly recapitulates both local and global arrangements, yielding experimentally informed ensembles that can inform structure-mediated function and resolve force field limitations. This can yield a fruitful exploration of ensemble-to-function relationships in IDPs, allowing to explore phenomena such as secondary structure propensity and nucleation in condensates, conformationally selected binding motifs across disordered ensembles or conformational preferences of sequence-specific short-linear motifs.

title: Mitochondrial subpopulations promote cellular responses to changes in metabolic demand and signal transduction
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: When mammalian cells are under increased ATP demand, mitochondria segregate into two distinct subpopulations, one capable of oxidative phosphorylation (oxidative subpopulation) and another specialized in reductive synthesis of metabolic precursors (reductive subpopulation). Here we report that mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) along with protein components of the mitochondrial nucleoid segregate to the oxidative subpopulation in response to increased ATP demand. This suggests that formation of the reductive mitochondrial subpopulation might serve to eliminate alternative uses of mitochondrial NAD(P)H when cells are under bioenergetic or nutrient stress. To examine this further, we studied mitochondria in cells exposed to low levels of glutamine. Mitochondria use glutaminase (GLS1) to maintain net glutamine uptake when cytosolic glutamine decreases, by converting glutamine to glutamate. The resulting glutamate can either be oxidized into α-ketoglutarate to enter the TCA cycle or utilized in the reductive synthesis of proline/ornithine. GLS1 can polymerize into hyperactive filaments in response to elevations in inorganic phosphate as might occur when ATP consumption exceeds production. However, when extracellular glutamine is reduced, GLS1 filaments segregated away from mtDNA, becoming colocalized with pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS) filaments in reductive mitochondria lacking ATP synthase markers. This cosegregation supported the ability of TGF-β signaling to enhance reductive proline/ornithine biosynthesis under low glutamine conditions despite compromising oxidative TCA cycle support from glutamine. The cosegregation of GLS1-P5CS filaments depended on continuing mitochondrial fission/fusion and occurred even in cells lacking mtDNA. Together, these data demonstrate that the reductive mitochondrial subpopulation is functional and under regulation by both metabolic demand and intercellular signal transduction.

title: Gene conversion is a key driver of diversity hotspots in Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens and virulence-associated loci
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Despite the long-held view of
                    Mycobacterium tuberculosis
                    (
                    Mtb
                    ) as a genetically conserved pathogen, many genomic regions remain poorly resolved due to high sequence homology and repetitive content. Using complete genome assemblies generated from long-read sequencing of 151 globally representative clinical isolates, we comprehensively analyzed genome-wide patterns of genetic diversity and evolution across the
                    Mtb
                    genome. Our analysis uncovers pronounced diversity hotspots within paralogous regions (PRs) generated by recurrent gene conversion between homologous genes. In many cases, these hotspots exhibit more than an order of magnitude greater genetic diversity than the rest of the
                    Mtb
                    genome, which is otherwise characterized by remarkably low variation. Mutations within these regions display clustered substitution patterns, excess paralog-matching variants, and distinct mutational spectra consistent with ongoing gene conversion. Our analysis identifies over 300 individual gene conversion events (GCEs) distributed throughout the
                    Mtb
                    phylogeny. These GCEs occur predominantly within gene families associated with virulence and host–pathogen interactions, including the PE, PPE, and ESX families. Several of the most pronounced diversity hotspots occur in antigens encoded within PRs. Among these, the vaccine candidate PPE18 harbors mutations in validated epitope sequences and predicted alterations in HLA-II binding. Together, these findings demonstrate that gene conversion actively shapes antigenic and virulence-associated diversity in
                    Mtb
                    .

title: Comparative analysis of photocatalytic, enzymatic, and chemical approaches to identify canonical and noncanonical surfaceomes
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: The cell surface is a critical nexus in cellular communication and a rich landscape yielding the majority of current therapeutic targets, yet only a small fraction of cell surface proteins have been targeted therapeutically. The cell surface proteome (surfaceome) comprises only ~1% of the human proteome by mass, motivating enrichment strategies to detect surfaceome alterations in disease for drug target discovery. Developments in photocatalytic technology have revolutionized the study of protein neighborhoods around specific targets of interest, but photocatalysis has been underutilized for global surfaceome analysis. Here, we describe five distinct photocatalytic surfaceomics strategies, all without the need for cellular engineering, that apply the photocatalyst Eosin Y attached to different cell surface structures: direct glycan ligation, glycan attachment via two different lectins, membrane insertion, and free in extracellular space. We systematically compare these photocatalytic surfaceomics methods to each other as well as to three established chemical and enzymatic surfaceomics methods. We demonstrate that the different photocatalytic surfaceomics techniques achieve broadly similar canonical cell surface protein enrichment but show some important differences reflective of cell surface attachment mechanism. These mechanistically orthogonal surfaceomics techniques consistently identified numerous nonglycosylated proteins with high concordance, many of which represent an underappreciated class of noncanonical cell surface proteins lacking traditional cell surface protein features that may represent potential drug targets. This study substantially expands options for surfaceomics methods using photocatalytic proximity labeling.

title: Random, fragile, or correlated: Mechanisms of synteny decay in mammals
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: We formalize three models of genome evolution, yielding analytical distributions of synteny block sizes between pairs of genomes. To evaluate each model, we fit theoretical synteny block size distributions to empirical distributions from a comparative analysis of nearly 200 mammalian genomes. Between the random breakage model (RBM), with uniformly distributed breakpoints, the fragile breakage model (FBM) with breakpoint hotspots, and what we term the correlated breakage model (CBM) with pairs of nearby breakpoints, we find that the FBM and CBM are far more consistent with mammalian genome evolution than the RBM. Inferred parameters of each model qualitatively agree with previously calculated rates of mammalian genome evolution. The FBM and CBM perform comparably with each other, suggesting that either model could serve as an improved null model of genome evolution to use in statistical tests for syntenic regions that are unlikely to exist due to random chance.

title: C1ql2 gates stress vulnerability by regulating microglia-mediated synaptic pruning in the BLA-vHPC circuit
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Synaptic remodeling in emotional circuits contributes to the development of stress-related emotional disorders. However, such remodeling generally exhibits considerable heterogeneity across specific neuronal populations and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identified
                    C1ql2
                    as a key molecular regulator that governs projection-specific synaptic vulnerability within basolateral amygdala (BLA). Transcriptional profiling revealed that
                    C1ql2
                    expression is enriched in BLA neurons projecting to ventral hippocampus (BLA
                    →vHPC
                    PNs), but not in those projecting to nucleus accumbens (NAc), and is significantly down-regulated following chronic social defeat stress (CSDS). Gain- and loss-of-function manipulations demonstrated that
                    C1ql2
                    regulates stress-induced neuronal remodeling in BLA
                    →vHPC
                    PNs, including dendritic hypertrophy, synaptic outgrowth, and enhanced glutamatergic transmission, thereby shaping susceptibility to anxiety-like behavior. We further found that CSDS-induced
                    C1ql2
                    loss impairs microglial engulfment of BLA
                    →vHPC
                    PNs synapses, leading to aberrant synaptic accumulation. Our findings establish C1ql2-mediated neuron-microglia cross talk that critically regulates circuit-specific synaptic pathophysiology in stress-related disorders.

title: Harry L. Swinney: Nonlinear science and chaos pioneer
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Harry Leonard Swinney passed away peacefully at his home in Austin, Texas, on July 13, 2026, at the age of 87. Harry was an exceptional experimental physicist, well-known for elegant studies of instabilities, nonlinear dynamics, chaos and pattern formation in a wide variety of fluid, chemical, and granular systems, work whose influence propagated into numerous scientific and engineering disciplines well beyond the particular problems that prompted it. The late Russell Donnelly of the University of Oregon used to say, “Harry is a prince”; Russ meant it, in the spirit of the tenth-century Persian poet Ferdowsi, as a compliment affirming the nobility, dignity, integrity, and grace with which Harry pursued his science and treated everyone he worked alongside.

title: Macromolecular association creates dispersity of components that determines liquid–liquid phase separation of oppositely charged polyions
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Developing insight into liquid–liquid phase separation in complex polyelectrolyte mixtures has acquired new urgency considering the role this process plays in the formation of biomolecular condensates, which are involved in diverse processes including, stress response, signal transduction, metabolism, gene regulation, and many human diseases. Condensates can be viewed as a biological membraneless structure situated, in scale and function, between macromolecules and cells. The physical properties of, and the physico-chemical environments within, condensates are very important determinants of their biological function. These properties and environments are determined by the phase separation process. Earlier experimental work in one of our laboratories characterized in detail a phase separation process in solutions of oppositely charged polypeptides. Considering new information being developed on macromolecular association in homogeneous solutions of oppositely charged polyions, we have revisited our earlier data looking into the influence of intermolecular association on the outcome of the phase transition. Such influence is clearly established in this Brief Report. We demonstrate that dispersity of species in homogeneous solution owing to macromolecular association affects phase separation by creating an open miscibility gap, leading to a dependence of the phase compositions on the initial polymer volume fraction. It is very likely that this plays a significant role in the formation of condensates in the biological context that may have been overlooked.

title: Structure of a sparsely populated chimeric intermediate that facilitates fold-switching of a metamorphic protein
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Metamorphic proteins challenge the single-sequence-structure-function paradigm by switching between distinct folds that often adopt complementary functions. However, the conformational states sampled along the fold-switching pathway have remained elusive because they are transient and unstable. Using multinuclear chemical exchange saturation transfer and relaxation dispersion NMR, combined with chemical shift–based structure determination and protein engineering, we visualized the atomic resolution structure of an “invisible” state of the metamorphic chemokine lymphotactin. This state is a chimera that integrates the secondary and tertiary structure of one fold with the quaternary assembly of the other. Locking lymphotactin into a single conformation abolishes access to this state, supporting its role as an on-pathway intermediate in metamorphosis. The stabilization of such hybrid intermediates is likely to have facilitated the evolution of fold-switching and represents a powerful strategy for protein design.

title: Multi-omics and spatial analysis of microgravity-grown glioblastoma organoids reveal superior modeling of advanced disease after long-term spaceflight
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Creating accurate organoid models remains a challenge, particularly for diseases like glioblastoma (GBM), an aggressive, treatment-resistant brain cancer with an immunosuppressive microenvironment. To overcome limitations of Earth-based models (sedimentation and disaggregation) and leverage the unique advantages of space (accelerated disease progression and immune dysregulation), this study utilizes a panel of GBM-myeloid organoids cultured for 40 d aboard the International Space Station. Spaceflight-grown GBM organoids have more uniform morphology compared to ground controls. We observed a context-dependent response to spaceflight, with the inclusion of macrophages and monocytes altering the bulk and spatial transcriptional response. While GBM-alone organoids have transcriptional markers of less aggressive disease in microgravity, organoids containing GBM cells + monocytes have increased expression of genes associated with disease progression and poor patient outcomes. Gene expression patterns are more spatially organized, with mesenchymal-related genes enriched in the core and inflammation-related genes enriched at the periphery, mimicking GBM tumor architecture. Microgravity-grown GBM+monocyte organoids exhibit increased secretion of proteins such as CXCL12 and LOX-1, associated with more aggressive disease. Infrared chemical imaging confirms spatial chemical gradients of DNA, protein, and lipid species in both space- and terrestrially-grown organoids. In summary, this work presents not only an advanced model of glioblastoma for basic and translational research but also demonstrates methods to acquire diverse data from organoids compatible with the unique constraints of in-space systems, helping establish a working model for orbital oncology.

title: IL36γ signaling promotes mammalian anti-tick immunity
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Ticks, like
                    Ixodes scapularis
                    , can parasitize a diverse array of vertebrates, favoring natural hosts but feeding opportunistically on others. Natural hosts, as well as permissive hosts such as laboratory mice, tolerate repeated infestations, while many incidental hosts may acquire anti-tick immunity, as first described in guinea pigs. We show that tick-immune guinea pigs display altered dermal cytology and a distinct transcriptome, predominantly upregulating the IL36γ cytokine. Interference with IL36γ signaling, via gene knockdown, chemical inhibition, or its natural antagonist IL36RN, reversed anti-tick immunity in guinea pigs. Conversely, genome engineering to silence IL36RN in C3H mice, representing a permissive host, disrupted tick engorgement, interfering with the transmission of Lyme disease pathogens. These findings firmly establish IL36γ as a central mediator of protective anti-tick immunity involving
                    I. scapularis
                    in mammalian hosts and support future strategies to interfere with tick-transmitted infections.

title: Anomalous narrow-band correlation in a natural superconducting heterostructure
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
A new frontier in condensed matter physics is to stack atomically thin layered materials with different properties and create intriguing phenomena which do not exist in any of the constituent layers. Transition metal dichalcogenide 4Hb-TaS
                    2,
                    with an alternating stacking of a spin liquid candidate 1T-TaS
                    2
                    and a superconductor 1H-TaS
                    2
                    , is a natural heterostructure for such a purpose. Recently, rare phenomena were indeed observed, including chiral superconductivity, two-component nematic superconductivity, topological surface superconductivity, and enigmatic magnetic memory. A widely proposed starting point to understand such a mysterious heterostructure requires strong electronic correlation, presumably provided by 1T-TaS
                    2
                    layers with a narrow flat band near the Fermi level (E
                    F
                    ). Here, by using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we reveal the theoretically expected flat band near E
                    F
                    in the energy-momentum space. However, this flat band only exists on the 1T-TaS
                    2
                    terminated surface layer with broken translational symmetry, but not on the 1T-TaS
                    2
                    subsurface layers buried in the bulk. These results directly challenge the foundation of the current theoretical paradigm. On the 1T-TaS
                    2
                    terminated surface layer, we further revealed a pseudogap and an anomalous doping effect. These phenomena and the dichotomy between surface and bulk layers also shed light on the unusual coexistence of distinct electronic orders in this mysterious heterostructure.

title: Compensation of the effects of temperature on a motor system in the crab, Cancer borealis
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Understanding how warming affects life-critical physiological processes is increasingly important as ocean temperatures rise at unprecedented rates. We study the stomatogastric system of the crab
                    Cancer borealis
                    . Movement depends on multiple temperature-sensitive processes, from motor pattern generation to neuromuscular transmission and contraction. Previous studies examined these levels separately and showed that warming increased pyloric rhythm frequency until the rhythm crashed at extreme temperatures. Here, we examined how the neuromuscular transform responds to this increase in motor neuron activity. We simultaneously recorded motor neuron activity, muscle fiber membrane potential, and contraction force. As temperature increased, the pyloric rhythm frequency increased, the excitatory junctional potential amplitudes remained constant, and muscle contraction diminished and failed. When muscles were stimulated at a fixed low frequency mimicking neuronal activity at cold temperatures, contraction decreased with acute warming. Increasing motor nerve stimulation frequency to mimic neuronal activity at warm temperatures partially rescued contraction. This shows that the temperature-dependent increase in neuronal firing provides partial compensation but is insufficient to prevent the loss of contraction at high temperatures. Because warming hyperpolarized muscle fibers, it moved the membrane potential further from the contraction threshold, and decreased synaptic integration, thus protecting against overexcitability. However, high-potassium-induced contractures revealed that the contractile machinery remained functional at high temperature, but the nerve-evoked depolarizations were apparently not large enough to cross the threshold for muscle contraction. Thus, a variety of temperature-dependent compensatory mechanisms overlap to extend the temperature range over which the neuromuscular system remains functional over a broad temperature range.

title: CD28 costimulation is organized by signaling condensates and counteracted by PD-1
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: T cell activation relies on the coordinated integration of T cell receptor (TCR) and cosignaling pathways, yet how these signals are physically organized remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that CD28 co-stimulation is driven by a condensation mechanism in which the CD28 intracellular domain (ICD) forms signaling condensates with the Src-family kinase Lck. Ligand engagement promotes CD28 ICD accessibility and triggers rapid CD28/Lck condensation, enhancing CD28 phosphorylation, cytoskeletal polarization, and cytokine production. The downstream effectors of CD28, including PI3K and GRB2, can also be recruited into the CD28-Lck condensates in our reconstituted system. We further identify PD-1 as a graded regulator of this process: Monophosphorylated PD-1 is recruited into CD28/Lck condensates, whereas diphosphorylated PD-1 competitively binds the CD28 ICD and dissolves these assemblies. CD28 and PD-1 ICDs also undergo condensation directly, revealing a dynamic and compositionally heterogeneous signaling system. Guided by this competitive condensation mechanism, we engineer CD28 ICD mutants that preserve Lck condensation while resisting PD-1-mediated disruption. Incorporation of these condensation-selective mutants into Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) constructs confers resistance to inhibitory signaling and enhances antitumor efficacy in vivo. These findings establish condensation as a central organizing principle of CD28 costimulation and provide a biophysical framework for engineering more resilient therapeutic T cells.

title: Mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation driven by energetic-particle irradiation of icy solids
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Mass-independent isotope fractionation (MIF) of oxygen provides key insights into atmospheric chemistry and the origin of isotopic anomalies in planetary materials. To date, MIF has been primarily associated with gas-phase processes involving symmetry-dependent reaction pathways, most notably ozone formation. Whether analogous effects can arise in condensed phases or at interfaces remains an open question. Here we report laboratory experiments demonstrating that energetic particle irradiation of icy oxide surfaces produces mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation at temperatures as low as 10 K. Electron irradiation of SiO
                    2
                    and Al
                    2
                    O
                    3
                    substrates in the presence of H
                    2
                    O ice results in measurable shifts in Δ
                    17
                    O in the underlying solids. The resulting three-isotope relationships include slope-1-like behavior in SiO
                    2
                    and Al
                    2
                    O
                    3
                    and distinct, substrate-dependent trends in Al
                    2
                    O
                    3
                    , indicating that irradiation-induced defect formation and interfacial chemistry govern the isotope effects. The magnitude of the observed anomalies demonstrates that irradiation-driven processes can generate substantial oxygen isotope heterogeneity in condensed phases. These results identify a previously unrecognized class of MIF and provide a quantitative framework for interpreting oxygen isotope signatures in radiation-processed environments, including interstellar grains and early solar system materials.

title: Unveiling the structure of Leishmania flagella through cryoelectron tomography
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Leishmania
                    are unicellular parasites that cause the serious disease leishmaniasis, presenting ongoing global challenges as existing treatments face issues with resistance and toxicity.
                    Leishmania
                    contain a single motile flagellum, essential for transmission, which has the conserved [9 + 2] microtubule arrangement. We used cryoelectron tomography to determine the ultrastructure of the
                    Leishmania tarentolae
                    96-nm repeat and paraflagellar rod. While the overall structure, including three broad radial spokes and two-headed outer dynein arms, resembles other eukaryotes like
                    Trypanosoma brucei, Tetrahymena,
                    and Opisthokonts, the
                    Leishmania
                    flagellum also exhibits unique and asymmetrical features. These include asymmetrically shaped radial spoke heads similar to
                    T. brucei
                    , suggesting this may represent a kinetoplastid-specific feature. Further,
                    Leishmania
                    contain an additional inner-junction and 8-nm wide A2 protofilament hole. Strikingly,
                    Leishmania
                    have many doublet-specific structures such as outer dynein arm tethers, interdoublet linkers, and heterogeneous connections to the paraflagellar rod. In this work, we show that divergent structural traits of
                    Leishmania
                    flagella highlight lineage-specific adaptations within eukaryotes.

title: Molecular fossils of an ancestral code revealed by large-scale analysis of tRNAs
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Modern tRNAs are thought to have evolved from simpler RNA minihelices resembling acceptor stems, some of which could be specifically aminoacylated. A central and testable prediction of minihelix-based models is that vestiges of ancestral coding relationships should remain embedded within the acceptor stems of contemporary tRNAs and should persist after correction for structural constraints. Here, we ask whether cognate anticodon-like triplets are statistically enriched in nonanticodon regions of modern tRNAs beyond what would be expected from structural and compositional constraints alone. Using a curated dataset of 77,335 canonical tRNA sequences and a structure-aware statistical framework, we find that for a subset of amino acids cognate anticodon-like triplets are significantly enriched in acceptor stems and, to a lesser extent, in other structural domains. Notably, these amino acids include those previously shown to support specific minihelix aminoacylation [Y. M. Hou, P. Schimmel,
                    Nature
                    333
                    , 140–145 (1988); C. Francklyn, P. Schimmel,
                    Nature
                    337
                    , 478–481 (1989)]. The strongest acceptor-stem signals survive structure-preserving null models, and cluster nonrandomly against proposed chronologies of amino acid incorporation into the genetic code. Together, these findings identify molecular fossils within modern tRNAs consistent with the persistence of an ancestral operational code, and provide refined statistical support for the notion that extant codon–amino acid relationships evolved from early aminoacylation systems involving RNA minihelices.

title: In-cloud motions shape warm-rain production in marine clouds: Evidence from multiyear observations
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Despite years of research, the processes controlling warm-rain formation remain uncertain. Leveraging multiple years of observations collected across four oceanic regions, we systematically reassess the properties of precipitation just beneath cloud base. The observations show that warm-rain characteristics are remarkably consistent within cloud regimes yet differ substantially between stratocumulus and cumulus, indicating that cloud-regime properties exert a stronger influence on warm precipitation than regional environmental variability. Precipitation is observed beneath marine stratocumulus in over 56% of cloudy columns with liquid water path (LWP) <130 g m
                    −2
                    , rising to more than 84% in columns with LWP beyond 130 g m
                    −2
                    . This indicates that marine stratocumulus routinely support warm-rain formation and suggests that barriers to precipitation onset in this regime are weaker than commonly assumed. For the same LWP, oceanic cumulus precipitate less frequently than stratocumulus but on average produce two times larger and one to two orders of magnitude fewer precipitation drops. This contrast is consistent with cumulus presenting two times stronger updrafts and lower adiabaticity than stratocumulus, both of which can affect drop growth histories. Whereas the precipitation characteristics of stratocumulus are generally consistent with growth by collision–coalescence during gravitational free fall in low LWP clouds, those of cumulus cannot be explained without invoking additional processes. Together, these findings suggest that warm-precipitation parameterizations should more explicitly account for the influence of small-scale dynamical processes on precipitation growth. The apparent importance of drop growth histories further motivates continued exploration of Lagrangian particle-tracking approaches in both models and observations.

title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners’ spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest within-network coherence, marking them as the central hub of the system, and distinguishing them from less central and less coherent domain-general regions. Together, the findings reveal how the brain dynamically decomposes complex spatial instruction, preserving parietal-centered spatial processing, while coordinating support from premotor, domain-general, and language systems. These findings begin to reveal how spatial cognition operates within the complexity of formal instruction.

title: Signal peptides for engineered protein secretion by free and hydrogel-encapsulated cyanobacteria
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Cyanobacteria provide a promising platform for light-driven heterologous protein production. In heterologous production systems, cells are typically lysed for product purification or to facilitate interaction with external substrates, unless the product is secreted. Fusion to molecular “shipping labels” known as signal peptides can target chimeric proteins to native membrane translocation pathways and result in secretion. In this work, we identified signal peptides from the model cyanobacterium
                    Synechococcus elongatus
                    PCC 7942 (
                    S. elongatus
                    ) and genetically fused to two heterologous enzymes: the reporter nanoluciferase (NLuc) and an oxidative laccase (CotA). Increased extracellular activity was observed for one or more signal-protein variants for both enzymes. Furthermore, cells of
                    S. elongatus
                    producing a signal-laccase chimera were encapsulated within an alginate hydrogel, and the resulting engineered living material released sufficient enzyme to decolorize a dye pollutant in its surroundings. These findings streamline recombinant protein production in cyanobacteria and facilitate environmental interactions with cell products, expanding the potential applications of both free-living and material-encapsulated cyanobacteria.

title: Programmable Structural Color Lifetimes via Activation Energy Engineering for Spatiotemporally Encoded Dynamic Optical Encryption
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Spatiotemporally programmable structural color holds great promise for high‐security optical encryption, yet precisely tailoring the lifetime of structural color across a broad temporal range spanning multiple orders of magnitude remains a significant challenge in polymer systems. The lifetime of structural color is intrinsically governed by the segmental relaxation kinetics of the underlying polymer network, which has been largely overlooked in the rational design. Here, we report a dynamic surface grating with programmable structural color lifetime, in which the optical evolution process is precisely encoded by tuning the activation energy through crosslinking density and amplitude control. Driven by segmental relaxation, the grating amplitude gradually decays over time, redistributing diffracted energy back to specular reflection and causing a gradual fading of structural color. By spatially encoding the relaxation activation energy via photomask‐assisted UV exposure, the structural color lifetime governed by local amplitude decay kinetics can be independently programmed across different regions, spanning an unprecedented temporal range from 300 s to over 240 days. This strategy enables diverse applications, ranging from stimulus‐responsive optical encryption and time‐resolved multilevel information encryption to practical cold‐chain integrity monitoring, establishing activation energy as a broadly applicable handle for temporal programmability in dynamic optical systems.

title: Supercapacitors Under Nonequilibrium Conditions: Mechanisms and Design Principles
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Supercapacitors have attracted considerable interest as high‐power energy storage devices for grid frequency regulation, backup power systems, and fast‐response applications, which are increasingly operated under conditions far from equilibrium, including floating states, high‐frequency cycling, rapid charge and discharge, wide temperature windows, and high‐voltage regimes. Under these nonequilibrium conditions, performance and stability are governed by coupled kinetic and thermodynamic processes, including ion transport limitations, interfacial polarization, electrolyte decomposition, and structural stress evolution. These processes span multiple length and time scales, from ion desolvation and surface reactions through pore‐level transport mismatch to macroscopic degradation. This review presents a unified perspective on the mechanisms that govern supercapacitor behavior under nonequilibrium conditions. Representative operating scenarios are analyzed to identify three common degradation origins, namely, transport mismatch, interfacial instability and thermo‐mechanical coupling. Building on this mechanistic understanding, rational material‐design principles are derived on ion transport regulation, interfacial chemistry regulation, electrolyte optimization, and structural adaptability. Finally, future research directions are discussed for bridging the gap between laboratory evaluation and real‐world operation and for guiding the development of robust supercapacitors for dynamic energy storage applications.
